newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Blueprint for EMU bond market seen taking shape.
newsitem.headline: Blueprint for EMU bond market seen taking shape.

text.p: Virtually all European Union governments are expected to redenominate their outstanding debt into a single currency with agreement on the nuts and bolts of the changeover expected by this summer.

EU officials say national governments and financial market practitioners are rapidly hammering out a blueprint for a euro bond market, considered by many as a critical step in securing the credibility of the euro.

The breadth and depth of such a market, dependent upon how many countries participate in economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, could eventually rival that of the U.S. government securities market, the world's largest.
"There is now broad agreement that debt should be redenominated at the start date," said one senior EU official.

Under the changeover scenario for EMU all new government debt will be denominated in the euro from the start date. But for outstanding debt, issued before the 1999 start date and due to mature sometime thereafter, governments were given the option to redenominate.

Both the European Commission and the Frankfurt-based European Monetary Institute -- forerunner to a European Central Bank -- have been engaged in talks with financial institutions on the best course of action.
The two institutions say rather than impose a specific plan on the markets, they have preferred to act as a forum for financial practitioners.

To be sure, several uncertainties remain, particularly with respect to whether private sector or corporate debt will be redenominated. This is a legally thorny area which some argue could give rise to numerous suits and unwanted complications.
In addition, there are legal differences between countries in how bond contracts are specified. The sharpest gaps appear to be between Britain and several continental countries.
But on the more positive side, officials say there is now broad recognition that uniform rules need to be agreed quickly in order to facilitate preparations.

A new study from the Bank of England, which borrows heavily from recent talks between banks and investment firms, noted that a decision on a common set of rules should be taken by July 1 of this year.

Importantly, officials say nearly all governments are expected to redenominate their outstanding debt, with the possible exception of the Netherlands, although even here there is the belief that the Dutch will come around.
Publicly, only three countries -- Belgium, France and Luxembourg -- have so far announced their intention to redenominate public debt from the outset in 1999.
All others within the 15-nation EU bloc are expected to make their intentions known within the coming months.
Among the various technical issues which need to be resolved officials say several areas of agreement have emerged.
For example, there is a consensus that market conventions -- the manner in which interest on bonds is calculated -- should be harmonised within the euro area.
Because of numerous public holidays which vary from one EU country to another, a common set of market conventions is needed in order to ensure the smooth functioning of a euro bond market.

For government bonds, it has been agreed that the preferred day count convention should reflect actual business days in each country during a given year, or what market practitioners commonly refer to as Actual/Actual.
With regard to the method used to redenominate outstanding debt various options are on the table, but the most favoured approach appears to be "simple redenomination."
According to the Bank of England's report, simple redenomination means that "a nominal amount in a national currency unit is re-stated as an exact amount in the euro unit at the conversion rate."
The rate at which national currencies will be converted into the euro will be announced in the spring of 1998, the same time as the selection of which countries join the single currency.
